arītu - Assyrian Dictionary p. 269,270

Babylonian Oracle (SAA 09 001 o iv 14-19):

maš-šur—PAB—AŠ ina URU.ŠÀ—URU UD-MEŠ ar-ku-u-ti MU-MEŠ da-ra-a-ti a-da-nak-⸢ka⸣
maš-šur—PAB—AŠ ina ŠÀ-bi URU.arba-⸢ìl⸣ a-ri-it-ka de-iq-tú a-[na-ku]

Esarhaddon! I will give you long days and everlasting years in the Inner City.
O Esarhaddon, I will be your good shield in Arbela.
State Archives of Assyria 09 001 o iv 19


Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet VIII, line 47 (Column ii, line 5) :

Gilgamesh's Lament for his friend Enkidu (in five translations):

R 47: nam-sar šiр-рі-iа [a-ri-t]u šá pa-ni-ia
e 47: nam-sar ši-bi-i a-ri-te šá ра-ni-iа

Hear me, O young men, hear [me!]
Hear me, O elders [of the populous city, Uruk,] hear me!
I shall mourn Enkidu, my friend,
like a professional mourning woman I shall lament bitterly.
The axe at my side, in which my arm trusted,’
the sword of my belt, the shield in front of me;8
my festive garment, the girdle of my delight:
a wicked wind has risen up against me and robbed me.

8 MS e adds (1. 47а): mu-kil li-du!?-x[...... ] 'who held ...[...... ]'.
Andrew George (2003)


Hear me, O young men, listen to me,
Hear me, O elders of [Uruk], listen to me!
I mourn my friend Enkidu,
I howl as bitterly as a professional keener.
Oh for the axe at my side, oh for the safeguard by my hand,
Oh for the sword at my belt, oh for the shield before me,
Oh for my best garment, oh for the raiment that pleased me most!
An ill wind rose against me and snatched it away!
Benjamin Foster (2001)

Hear me, O Elders of Uruk, hear me, O men!
I mourn for Enkidu, my friend,
I shriek in anguish like a mourner.
You, axe at my side, so trusty at my hand--
you, sword at my waist, shield in front of me,
you, my festal garment, a sash over my loins--
an evil demon!) appeared and took him away from me!
Kovacs (1989)

Listen to me, Elders. Hear me out, me.
I [have been] to [you], Enkidu, your mother, your father; I will weep for you in the wilderness.
For Enkidu, for my friend, I weep like a wailing woman, howling bitterly.
[He was] the axe at my side, the bow at my arm,
the dagger in my belt, the shield in front of me,
my festive garment, my splendid attire . . .
An evil has risen up and robbed me.
Gardner / Maier (1984)

Hear me, great ones of Uruk,
I weep for Enkidu, my friend,
Bitterly moaning like a woman mourning
I weep for my brother.
O Enkidu, my brother,
You were the axe at my side,
My hand's strength, the sword in my belt,
The shield before me,
A glorious robe, my fairest ornament;
An evil Fate has robbed me.
N.K. Sandars (1977)
